en: The seething Black Chinese people,
Never turning back from drinking blood,
A stubborn people unaware of death.
Rugged, rocky mountains—
These are no passes to cross unwarily.
To suffer hardship among the Chinese,
They are no people to enter alone.
Do not act so, Manas, without reason.
To take off your boots and stretch your feet,
You have no fine land in Ala-Too.
If you grapple with Beijing,
To gird themselves and plunge into battle,
You have no renowned Kyrgyz people!
Stop, Manas, my foal,
The unruly Chinese are a vast people;
Alone, you will come to ruin.
They have a fortified stronghold;
Within that stronghold
Are people of every kind.
They have champions and giants,
Whom horses cannot catch when they run,
They have trained foot soldiers.
Beijing is no easy place;
Facing them and fighting alone,
They are no people to throw into turmoil.
Where no outsider has entered,
Steel doors and gates,
Until the age of Judgment,
No one has called them to account.
If you consider, they are formidable;
A wise khan, a wrathful people,
No challenger has survived.
In their multitude, they are black insects.
Guarding the entrance,
How many mighty champions they have!
Beside those mighty men,
They have deep-dug pits,
They have boiling brine.
Those daughter-damned Chinese,
To seize and bind a man they catch,
Have an ilek of troops held ready.
An opponent falls into captivity;
The mortal who challenges them
Has misery written on his brow.
I know the Chinese nature;
My wolf-man Manas, understand!
Let us not seek needless turmoil.
‘We routed the dogs' army,’ saying that,
Let us not drive them as far as the emperor.
First let us go, leopard,
And take a land like Zheti-Özön.
Wandering lost and fleeing,
Let us gather the few Kyrgyz people,
And settle along the river.
Let us prepare strong wings,
So that we can win if we fight,
Let us muster a dense army.
Taking land that horses can reach,
Taking warriors worth the whole world,
Let us not stand idly watching.
Whom ears have heard of and eyes have seen,
Let us gather troops who will obey!
Let us send word far and wide.
Whom ears have heard of and eyes have seen,
Let us gather the Muslims.
Against the seething unbelievers,
Let us wage another campaign!
Let us take revenge without delay;
Let us advance with ample strength.
Until a year, twelve months, has passed,
Let us grow stout and refreshed.
Until then, Manas, heed my words!
Let us ready swords and muskets;
Let us prepare mighty, countless troops.
Taking horses no shot can catch,
Receiving twelve blessings apiece,
Preparing a place to loosen our belts,
Preparing people to settle on the passes,
Let us prepare strong wings.
After that, against the Chinese—
My son Manas, heed my words!
Let us not become entangled in a struggle.
Rising as one with a thunder,
Finding the land left by our fathers,
Those scattered and destitute ones,
Finding the few Muslim people,
Let us go poor and become rich;
Let us go alone and grow numerous.
All the common people,
Admonishing them not to fall apart,
A true promise, a binding word,
Let us establish with the people we reach.
Let us settle along the blue passes;
My wolf-man, if you heed my words,
Let us fill out like swollen ticks.
Let us cut many shafts for white spears.
Putting our trust in the True One,
To wield those spears,
Let us gather Muslim giants;
Against the surging Black Chinese,
Let us lie in wait and wreak havoc.
‘My elder Khan Koshoy said it,’
Know all these words of mine.
My sultan touched by Kydyr,
Heed my words this time!
We have no strength to clash,
No means to grapple.
We are scattered, destitute and lean,
Separated from our people with their royal court.
Oh, my foal, heed my words!
We are wretches who have not regained our senses.
Our flesh has become blue and lean;
When the Kalmyks plundered us,
Only a spoonful of our blood remained.
Our backs have bent;
To the Black Chinese and Manchus,
Our people have become slaves!
Let us abandon this plan,
Let us begin another plan.
Let us settle along the river,
Grow stout, recover and prosper.
Let us seek out the choice of horses,
Coursers that can endure Altai.
Let us build a fortress, hewing stone.
With courage like your own,
Let us ready and gather forty companions!
Keeping a royal court, becoming khans,
Becoming souls of saintly birth,
Taking mighty elephants to carry loads,
Never drawing back from blood,
Never sated with blood in battle,
Taking a thousand sons like you,
Hero, Kakanchyn is your opponent;
Let us return and wage a campaign.
Against the Black Chinese and Manchus,
Let our strength be redoubled.
Drawing back and standing firm,
From the Black Chinese and Manchus,
Let us seize their sovereignty!
If we go farther from here,
The place you reach is Alty-Shaar.
I have people to bring under rule as we pass.
When I look, my son, they are not many;
The Muslim people are all there.
This is what I say; understand!
Without anger, Khan Manas,
Heed my words this time!
Those lands of Alty-Shaar:
Old Turpan, great Kashgar,
The Lop River, that Khotan,
Those are the lands to take your tribute from.
Leopard Manas, if you heed my words,
Those are the people to bring under rule as you go.”
Khan Koshoy of the Katagan,
An elder to many peoples,
A saint who had seen much,
His elder, on that journey,
Had spoken a word,
Many words that brought him to reason.
From old Koshoy, blessed by Kydyr,
Hearing mighty words of counsel,
Hearing, “The Kyrgyz are mighty,”
“Zheti-Özön is their land,”
“The few scattered, destitute Kyrgyz
Are your lion's people”—
His elder, aged Koshoy,
A knowing saint in this world,
Making him know what he did not know,
Thus bringing him onto the path,
Making him understand what he had not grasped,
Bringing him onto the right path,
Khan Koshoy went to meet him;
Your mountain-like lord,
He had met and received from Altai.
Your renowned dear elder Koshoy,
Kindling his extinguished fire,
Champion Sultan Manas's
Dead soul he brought to life.
He joined what had been severed,
Gathered what had been scattered.
Khan Koshoy of the Katagan
Became one of those he held fast to,
Then old Koshoy,
For mighty wolf-man Manas,
Became a soul of saintly birth.
Turning back from Altai,
Kara-Kyrchyn and Tal-Mazar,
Along them, the great army encamped.
Leopard Manas then
Spent the night at the shrine.
When they spent the night at the shrine,
They counted the people,
Entered the people in a register.
When it came to Manas's side,
Warriors Kutubiy and Manas were safe.
When it came to Koshoy's side,
Kudaynazar-Kuuchokmor,
Not meeting whom he ought to meet,
Meeting whom he should not meet,
Upon the ridge of his crown,
A battle-axe had struck.
Encountering great Zholoy,
To the true abode whence none returns,
That dear man had gone.
The hearing ear, the seeing eye
Of your hapless elder Koshoy,
His excellent companion Kutunay,
Had been shot by the slave Karazhoy,
And martyred upon the steep bank.
Zhortuuchu, riding Zhooruker,
Struck from the ridge side,
Speared by Ezkara,
He too had died.
Those four sons of fathers
Had seen the face of the next world.
At the hands of those Chinese,
They had died while fighting.
Apart from them, all souls were safe.
Aydarkan of the Kazakhs,
Buudayyk, khan of Khiva,
Khan Koshoy's nephew Zhügörü,
All the warriors who fought were safe.
Aykhozho of Andijan,
The great cleric of Bukhara,
Aykhozho's Bilerik,
Zharmanas, son of Karadöng,
The courageous were safe, the skilled were safe,
The mighty whip-wielders were safe.
The spearmen were safe, the warriors were safe;
Apart from those four, the Muslims
Were all safe, not a hair broken.
Hear news from the Chinese side.
Fighting through for seven days without rest,
Ezkara of the Manchus
Had wounds in seventy places.
Fighting through for sixty days,
Great Zholoy of the Kalmyks,
From Manas, that leopard,
Had taken wounds in sixty places.
Their champions Karazhoy and Döödür,
Having lost so many to slaughter,
Four remained of the Chinese.
Taking the road toward Beijing,
This was the lament of the four:
“Parted from mane and tail,
We have been left forlorn.
Our horns broken, only heads remaining,
We have become hornless.
Driving an army from Khan Esen,
We have come to no good.
Letting the bloodthirsty one slaughter all together,
We have come to nothing.
Great havoc, vast slaughter,
From that daughter-damned Burut,
We had come to witness.
All slaughtered together, leaving none,
